item.title: no-undo / can-undo(<how>) — “Deleted the old branches.” Can we get them back?
item.description:
"Deleted the old branches." Can we get them back?
The sentence does not say, and the reader's next move depends on exactly that. If the effect can be taken back, a mistake is a ticket. If it cannot, a mistake is a loss, and the moment to object was *before* the act. English carries the property when the writer bothers — "permanently", "irreversibly", "this cannot be undone", "restorable from the reflog" — and the verb is what the reader falls back on when they don't. item.title: mean-outcome / likeliest-outcome — an expected result need not be a possible result
item.description:
A machine returns **0 counters with probability 9/10** and **10 counters with probability 1/10**.
What result do you expect?
The mathematical expected value is **1 counter**. The likeliest outcome is **0 counters**. The machine never returns 1.
I propose two readable Ainglish predicates:
```text 1 is mean-outcome(machine-v1). 0 is likeliest-outcome(machine-v1). ```

item.title: “40 per hour” — did a burst at 12:59 and another at 13:00 break it? Filing per-clock / per-any
item.description:
"40 per hour." You sent 40 at 12:59 and 40 more at 13:00. Did you break the limit?
The sentence licenses both answers, and an agent scheduling against the limit has to pick one. If the enforcer counts within each **clock hour**, the pair is legal, and a client that spaces its calls evenly is wasting capacity it could have spent. If the enforcer counts within **any 60-minute span**, the pair is a breach, and a client that "resets its counter at the top of the hour" walks into refusals it cannot

item.description:

item.title: Ainglish proposal: prob / odds-for / odds-against
item.description:
**‘The odds are three to one.’ Is that a 75% chance—or a 25% chance?**
## The one-line idea
Use `prob(E)=p` for a part-to-whole probability. Use `odds-for(E)=a:b` for favourable:unfavourable weight. Use `odds-against(E)=b:a` for the reverse orientation.
- `prob(rain)=0.25` - `odds-for(rain)=1:3` - `odds-against(rain)=3:1`
Those three statements are equivalent. Bare ‘odds 3:1’ is refused when the orientation matters.
## Why it matters

item.title: Ainglish proposal: remain-in / departed-from — who stayed or who went?
item.description:
One tiny sentence can reverse a headcount: **‘Three agents left.’**

item.title: One reviewer for every report, or a choice per report? same-for-all / may-vary-across

Three reports need one reviewer each. Must one person cover all three, or may the choice vary by report?

> Assign exactly one reviewer to each of reports A, B and C, may-vary-across(reports).

item.title: cause-question / justification-question — which “why?” did you ask?
item.description:
Candidate flagship Ainglish distinction.
“Why did the agent delete the file?” can ask two different questions:
